title: What is Mutual Assured Destruction?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain mutual assured destruction (MAD), the Cold War nuclear strategy in which the US and Soviet Union kept enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other, so that a first strike would guarantee a retaliatory strike. They cover early Cold War scares (the Cuban missile crisis and a NORAD computer glitch that falsely showed an incoming Soviet attack), nuclear parity and proliferation, Eisenhower and Thomas Schelling's deterrence argument, Henry Kissinger's use of game theory, the ladder of escalation, the detente standoff, and the prisoner's dilemma as an analogy, with a tangent to the film WarGames. The episode closes with listener mail about a traditional horn-branding headache remedy in Sapa, Vietnam.

segments.title: Opening banter and Punkin Chunkin plugs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about hats, a Discovery/Science Channel Thanksgiving broadcast of Punkin Chunkin, and Chuck's past work on the topic for another show.

segments.title: Introducing mutual assured destruction
segments.summary: Josh introduces mutual assured destruction (MAD) as a Cold War strategic doctrine. The hosts reflect on growing up as Cold War kids with the threat of nuclear war.

segments.title: Cuban missile crisis and NORAD computer glitch
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Cuban missile crisis, when Soviet missiles in Cuba threatened the US, and a NORAD false alarm in which a computer display showed an apparent incoming Soviet strike, later revealed to be a glitch, during a seven-minute decision window.

segments.title: Nuclear parity, proliferation and deterrence
segments.summary: Both superpowers built up nuclear arsenals, each matching the other, so that each could destroy the other several times over. Eisenhower's view changed after Thomas Schelling argued that nuclear weapons were a deterrent, including against conventional war.

segments.title: Game theory and the balance of terror
segments.summary: Henry Kissinger's interest in game theory and its application to nuclear strategy is discussed. Robert McNamara's point that each side must believe the other will retaliate is described. The resulting uneasy truce, called detente, is explained.

segments.title: Early bombs and the ladder of escalation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss early bombs Fat Man and Little Boy and how warheads became more precise. They describe the ladder of escalation, in which each strike invites a counterstrike and the risk of moving up toward full nuclear war.

segments.title: WarGames and the prisoner's dilemma
segments.summary: The hosts tie the ladder of escalation to the film WarGames, whose lesson is that the only way to win is not to play. They explain the prisoner's dilemma as a related game theory exercise.

segments.title: Further reading
segments.summary: Josh suggests readers search for mutual assured destruction on the site and read Tom Shreeve's game theory article.

segments.title: Listener mail: horn-branding headache remedy in Vietnam
segments.summary: A listener describes a trip to Sapa, Vietnam, where a host served rice wine and demonstrated a traditional headache remedy of branding the forehead with a heated cow's horn. The hosts invite Cold War and unicorn stories.
